To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the prevalence of hypertension in the population was 29.1% and was associated with age, sex, and education, but not with deprivation, and the prevalence of hypertension was 38.7% among patients in primary health care.
the prevalence of hypertension was significantly higher among individuals with low income and low education.

the incidence of hypertension was positively associated with neighborhood-level socioeconomic deprivation, as measured by the Townsend index, and that these associations were stronger in women than in men.

the association between social deprivation and incident hypertension.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results from the present study suggest that the use of different sources of information on incident hypertension can lead to different results in terms of the association of socioeconomic position (SEP) with incident hypertension.
the associations between neighborhood deprivation and incident hypertension differ based on the source of case identification.
the association between deprivation and incident hypertension was divergent based on different sources for case identification.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the association between socioeconomic status and incident hypertension is not universal, but rather depends upon how the case definition is defined and the source of the data.
there are significant disparities in the incidence of hypertension among people with and without disabilities.
the associations between deprivation and hypertension differ when cases of hypertension are identified using different sources.
